issues.legal_issue: A constitutional writ petition is not maintainable to resolve a disputed property-possession claim between private parties when the dispute can be determined through ordinary proceedings and no breach of statutory duty by a public authority is alleged.
material_facts: The claimant sought restoration of possession of a flat through a writ petition against another private individual and public authorities.
The private individuals disputed their rights to ownership and possession of the flat, including whether the claimant had been in possession.
A civil suit concerning the flat was already pending, and a civil suit was available to determine the parties’ claims.
No violation of a statutory duty by a public authority was alleged as the basis for the possession claim.
issues.conclusion: The writ petition was not maintainable and should have been dismissed; the parties remained free to pursue appropriate civil proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, extraordinary writ jurisdiction is not a substitute for ordinary civil or criminal remedies for disputes between private persons. Property-rights and possession questions requiring determination of disputed facts and evidence are for the competent ordinary court. Article 226 may support directions to a statutory authority where breach of a statutory duty is alleged. The Court relied on Mohan Pande v. Usha Rani, (1992) 4 SCC 61, and Dwarka Prasad Agrawal v. B.D. Agrawal, (2003) 6 SCC 230; it also noted that a possession dispute may be decided in civil proceedings or proceedings under Section 145 CrPC.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_for_property_possession and private_parties_dispute_property_rights and possession_or_ownership_facts_are_disputed and ordinary_court_remedy_available and not statutory_duty_breach_alleged

predicates.constitutional_writ_for_property_possess: A claimant brought a constitutional writ petition seeking possession-related relief concerning property.
predicates.private_parties_dispute_property_rights: Private individuals asserted competing rights to ownership or possession of the property.
predicates.possession_or_ownership_facts_are_disput: The parties disputed facts about ownership, possession, or the circumstances of possession.
predicates.ordinary_court_remedy_available: An ordinary civil or criminal proceeding was available to determine the relevant dispute.
predicates.statutory_duty_breach_alleged: The claimant alleged that a public authority breached a statutory duty in a way material to the relief sought.

issues.definition: When a property-possession writ concerns competing private rights and disputed facts that an ordinary court can determine, and no relevant statutory-duty breach is alleged, the writ claim is not maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: A writ court exceeds its jurisdiction by deciding disputed factual questions about private property possession and ordering restoration of possession on that basis.
material_facts: The writ court determined that the claimant had been in possession of the flat and ordered the other private individual to restore possession.
The parties disputed who possessed the flat and their respective ownership and possession rights.
Resolving those questions required assessment of evidence in an ordinary civil proceeding, and possession disputes could also be addressed through the applicable criminal proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The writ court was not justified in making factual findings and ordering restoration of possession; its order was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The extraordinary jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution is not to be used to decide disputed property facts that require evidence or to convert a writ petition into a civil suit. A possession dispute between private individuals must be determined through an appropriate ordinary proceeding, including a civil suit or, where applicable, proceedings under Section 145 CrPC. The Court relied on Mohan Pande v. Usha Rani, (1992) 4 SCC 61, and Dwarka Prasad Agrawal v. B.D. Agrawal, (2003) 6 SCC 230, concerning the limits of writ jurisdiction and the availability of ordinary remedies.
